instructions: t3term is a Rust terminal client for T3 Code's orchestrator V2 (protocol 2). It is one binary: with no arguments it opens a ratatui TUI, and its subcommands form a CLI. It connects to the T3 server already running on the machine. It never starts a server or opens T3's database. Its purpose is to replace the Electron desktop app with a client that uses far less CPU, memory and energy while still behaving like T3, so idle CPU and per-command cost are requirements, not polish. Layout: discovery.rs finds the server from ~/.t3/userdata/server-runtime.json and checks the protocol version. auth.rs issues and revokes bearer sessions through the server's own `t3 auth session` command and keeps one 30-day login per environment in the macOS Keychain through keychain.rs. http.rs and rpc.rs speak HTTP and Effect RPC over one /ws WebSocket, with chunk acks and pings. client.rs holds the operations the CLI and TUI share. Its watchers resubscribe after a dropped connection. The shell and thread streams resume with afterSequence, and subscribeServerConfig has no cursor, so it starts again from a fresh snapshot. subscribeWorktreeSetup takes {threadId} and has no cursor either. Each of its items is the thread's whole setup or null, so a resubscribe starts again from the current setup. projection.rs reduces V2 events into thread state. transcript.rs turns thread items into blocks that the CLI prints and the TUI styles. models.rs checks model, effort and mode choices against the server's config. settings.rs keeps t3term's own preferences in ~/.config/t3term/settings.json. main.rs is the CLI, with documented exit codes and --json output. src/tui/ is the TUI. tests/fake_server.rs runs the real RPC client against a fake server, and tests/cli.rs runs the built binary with a temporary home against fake servers on 127.0.0.1. `.claude/skills/` holds the agents' verification procedures. verify-t3term's scripts/t3v drives the built binary in tmux against fake servers on 127.0.0.1, and its features/ files say how to reach and drive each feature. docs/parity.md is the feature plan pinned to one T3 nightly, and docs/sprint.md records the PRs that build it. research/ and benchmarks/ hold measurements and the scripts that produced them. Wire formats and field names come from T3's TypeScript source (pingdotgg/t3code), so a change to them should say which T3 file or recorded event it matches. Review for correctness and credential safety first, then for CPU and memory cost, then for clarity. macOS is the only supported platform for now, and Linux or Windows code must not change the macOS build. Point out claims in README.md or research/ that the code or measurements in the PR do not support. PRs that change how the TUI looks include screenshots or recordings. Review those for behavior, not visual taste.

rules.rule: Bearer tokens must never appear in argv, logs, error messages, panic messages, Debug output or --json output, and must never be written to disk outside the Keychain. Keychain writes pass the secret to /usr/bin/security on stdin. Flag any new path that formats, prints or stores a token, and any struct holding a token without a Debug impl that redacts it.

Every session t3term issues must end up either saved in the Keychain or revoked before the process exits, on every exit path: normal return, error, Ctrl+C, SIGHUP from a closed terminal and SIGTERM. A spawned revoke must be waited for, or tracked so exit waits for it, and must not die with the terminal's process group. Concurrent t3term processes must not issue duplicate saved logins. Flag new exit paths (process::exit, panics, early returns from main) that skip revoke_all_sessions.

The saved login and every other session the CLI and TUI log in with carry only the orchestration:read and orchestration:operate scopes and last at most 30 days. The one exception is the terminal session that src/client/terminal_access.rs issues on the first terminal connection. It carries only terminal:read and terminal:operate, lasts at most 12 hours and is never saved. Flag a terminal scope in any other session, any other new scope, any longer TTL, and any HTTP or RPC call that needs more access than the session it uses grants.

t3term must not open or write T3's SQLite databases or other files under ~/.t3, except reading server-runtime.json. It must not start, stop, restart or signal the T3 server or desktop app. It talks to T3 only through the server's HTTP and WebSocket API and the server's own `t3 auth session` commands.

Method names, message shapes, field names and enum values must match T3 orchestrator V2 protocol 2 as defined in T3's TypeScript source. This covers the fields the CLI, models.rs, transcript.rs and the TUI read from snapshots, events and server config, as well as what the client sends. Flag field names that look guessed, fields T3 requires that are left out, and enum string literals that are neither cited nor tested. The client must keep acking stream chunks and keep the 10-second ping and the 30-second dead-socket timeout. After a reconnect, orchestration.subscribeShell and orchestration.subscribeThread resume with afterSequence. subscribeServerConfig has no cursor, so it resubscribes with an empty payload and starts again from the snapshot T3 sends first. subscribeWorktreeSetup sends {threadId} alone. Each item is a whole setup snapshot or null, and a resubscribe sends the same payload with no cursor and starts from the current state. A setup's sequence counts the changes of that one setup, so it can start over or go lower after a null or a reconnect. The watcher passes setup items on as T3 sent them. Don't ask it to drop repeated setup items or to send a cursor for them. The client must refuse servers that do not report protocol 2.

V2 events carry the whole updated entity, so the reducer upserts it by id. Applying an event a second time, as happens after a reconnect, must leave state unchanged. Flag reducer changes that merge partial fields, depend on arrival order beyond sequence numbers, or can append a message or activity twice.

Thread titles, messages, tool output and file paths come from the server and from coding agents, so treat them as untrusted. Flag places where that text reaches the terminal, in CLI output or TUI cells, without removing escape and control characters that could move the cursor, redraw the screen or set the clipboard. The TUI must restore the terminal (raw mode, alternate screen, mouse capture) on every exit path, including panics and signals.

Low CPU and memory use is the reason t3term exists. The TUI draws after input, a server event or a due timer. A frame that only needs drawing waits until 33 ms have passed since the last one, so the TUI draws at most 30 times a second. A layout change, such as hiding, showing or resizing the sidebar, draws at once, so sizes and click targets match the screen. Besides that wait, two timers can wake it. A one-second tick runs only while a clock or spinner it shows is moving: a run in the open thread, a running setup card in view, or a Working or Goal card the sidebar drew. A one-shot timer fires when the soonest snooze ends. Each frame copies only the visible rows. Flag timers or polling loops that wake while idle, a tick kept for a clock that is off screen or has stopped, redraws that none of these caused, rewrapping or re-rendering the whole transcript on each frame, per-frame allocations that grow with transcript length, and caches without a bound. Flag work that builds an unchanged banner or the thread details again on an unrelated stream update or redraw, and trimming, cleaning, width or grapheme work over huge text before it is cut to a bound. In the CLI, `watch`, `wait` and `send --wait` handle every event of a stream. Flag work beyond a cheap check that each event repeats for items already printed, such as describing them again or looking up their runs, and history that `read` formats more than once per item.

Code on the tokio runtime must not block. Keychain calls, std::process, std::fs and file locks belong in spawn_blocking or a tokio equivalent. External commands and network calls need timeouts. Child processes need kill_on_drop or explicit tracking. Data from the server must not be unwrapped or indexed in ways that panic on unexpected input.

Scripts and agents depend on the CLI. Exit codes must stay as README.md documents them: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 usage, 3 not found, 4 rejected or unsupported protocol, 5 server unavailable, 6 timeout, 7 waiting for an approval or answer. With --json, stdout carries only JSON: one object per command, or one per line for watch, with errors as {"ok": false, "error": {"code", "message"}}. Flag changes to commands, flags, output fields or exit codes that README.md does not reflect.

The TUI should behave like the T3 desktop app: the same thread list, transcript order, approval and question flows, and the same names for providers, models, modes and statuses. Flag key bindings that clash with existing ones or are missing from README.md, and behavior that differs from the desktop app without a stated reason.

macOS is the only supported platform. Linux gets an optional build and test job in CI. Linux or Windows code must sit behind cfg gates that leave the macOS build and behavior unchanged, and features that need the macOS Keychain must fall back to a temporary session elsewhere. Flag hard-coded home directories and other machine-specific paths.

The t3v driver under .claude/skills/verify-t3term/scripts runs t3term against fake servers it starts itself, so it can run on any machine without touching the user's T3. It binds 127.0.0.1 only and never connects to a real T3 server. It runs t3term under env -i with a temporary HOME and T3CODE_HOME and T3TERM_NO_SAVED_LOGIN=1, and it never reads the real ~/.t3, the Keychain or a .env file. It signals only processes it started, after checking their command line, and deletes only run directories it created and marked. Evidence directories survive cleanup. Flag a path that binds another address, reads the user's home, kills or deletes by name or pattern, or writes a bearer token to argv, a log or evidence.

The files under .claude/skills/verify-t3term/features/ tell a verifier how to reach and drive each feature of the TUI and CLI, by the keys, labels and texts a user sees. A pull request that changes a key, a label, a click target, a status word or a flow a user sees updates the feature file that names it, or adds one and lists it in features/README.md. Flag a changed key binding or on-screen label that a feature file still names the old way, and a feature file that names a t3v command or flag the driver doesn't have.

CPU, memory, latency and energy numbers in docs, and the counts of requests or output bytes a verification page reports, must come from a measurement that benchmarks/ can reproduce or that the PR describes. Flag numbers a PR adds or changes without saying how they were measured and what that method can't show, and scripts that hard-code a user's home directory.
